notes.meaning: David cries out to God for mercy because dangerous enemies are pursuing him. He had fled to the Philistine city of Gath, only to find himself surrounded by foes who wanted to devour him. Knowing he cannot save himself and will receive no pity from people, he pleads for God's free grace.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine taught that the believer faces two enemies here: visible persecutors and the unseen devil. He saw being pressed down as like grapes being trodden to produce wine.

notes.meaning: David's enemies track him relentlessly all day long. They attack him with arrogance from positions of power, eager to swallow him up. In his weakness, he looks up to God, who sits far higher than the proudest earthly ruler.

David admits that he feels real fear when danger closes in. Instead of giving up, he makes a deliberate choice to place his confidence in the Lord. Choosing to trust God is the best remedy when fear grips our hearts.

David praises God for His dependable promises and finds deep peace in them. He realizes that his attackers are only frail, mortal human beings made of flesh, while God is all-powerful. Because the Lord protects him, no human being can bring him ultimate harm.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that early Greek translations read 'my words' instead of 'his word,' taking the phrase to mean praising God with one's own speech.

notes.meaning: David's adversaries constantly twist what he says to make him look guilty. They take his innocent words and distort their meaning to turn others against him. Their minds never stop plotting ways to bring about his ruin.

The wicked band together in secret to plan David's death. They shadow his movements and spy on every step he takes, waiting for a chance to take his life. David brings these hidden plots into the open before God.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine viewed these lurking enemies as a picture of false brethren hiding inside the church, pointing to Judas as the prime example.

notes.meaning: David asks whether these wicked men can really escape God's justice through their evil plots. He knows that no amount of cunning can shield the ungodly from the Lord's righteous anger. He prays for God to bring down the proud nations that oppose His work.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Following an early Latin translation, Augustine read this verse as God saving people without any merits of their own, and urged believers to pray for the salvation of their enemies.

notes.meaning: David comforts himself with the truth that God tracks every step of his wanderings as an exile. He asks God to gather all his tears as if storing them in a flask and writing them down in a permanent scroll. God notices every sorrow His children suffer and will never forget their pain.
David expects his enemies to turn and run the moment he cries out to God in prayer. Prayer unleashes divine help that no human power can resist. He lives in full assurance that God is on his side.

David repeats his praise of God's promise to steady his own heart. He uses both the general title 'God' and the personal covenant name 'the LORD' to honor His faithfulness. Praising God's promises in advance builds our faith before the rescue even arrives.

David firmly declares once more that his trust rests in God alone. Because his faith is fixed on the Almighty, he refuses to give in to fear. Mortal people may boast of great strength, but they have no ultimate power over someone God protects.

During his days of danger, David made solemn vows to honor God when deliverance came. Now he gladly prepares to bring his thank offerings and keep the promises he made. He views thanksgiving not as an afterthought, but as a joyful debt of love owed to God.

God has rescued David from the edge of the grave and kept his feet from stumbling into ruin. As a result, David is spared to walk in God's presence and enjoy the bright gift of life. The Lord delivers His servants so they may live before Him in thankful obedience.
